title: Ending the Debt Trap
overview: While the wall is being rebuilt, poor families cry out that wealthy fellow Jews are profiting from their hunger, and Nehemiah forces the lenders to stop and points to his own example.

parts.label: The poor cry out (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Famine and the Persian king's tax pushed poor families to borrow, putting up their land as security and even handing over their children as servants to pay debts. Their protest is that the lenders are their own people, and their children are worth no less.

parts.label: Nehemiah confronts the lenders (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: The law of Moses forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite in need, yet the leading families were doing just that, perhaps one percent a month, though scholars are unsure of the exact rate. Nehemiah points out the bitter irony: they had paid to free Jews sold abroad, and now these leaders were selling their own people into debt slavery.

parts.label: A public oath (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: The lenders agree to return the land and the interest, and Nehemiah makes them swear it before the priests. He shakes out the fold of his robe, which people used as a pocket, as a picture of how God would empty out anyone who broke the promise.

parts.label: Nehemiah's own example (vv. 14-18)
parts.note: For twelve years as governor, Nehemiah refused the food allowance he was entitled to collect, unlike earlier governors who taxed the people heavily. He fed a large table of officials and guests from his own wealth, likely earned in his high post at the Persian court.

parts.label: A prayer to be remembered (v. 19)
parts.note: Nehemiah closes by asking God to remember the good he has done for the people. Short prayers like this appear several times in his account.

think: When someone in need borrows from someone better off, what do you think the lender owes them beyond simply getting the money back?
